subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) is the most common type of porphyria, characterized by photosensitive skin lesions. It results from a deficiency in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, an enzyme in the heme synthesis pathway. This leads to an accumulation of porphyrin precursors in the skin.

sections.p: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) is a metabolic disorder affecting the heme synthesis pathway. It is the most prevalent form of porphyria globally. The primary clinical manifestation is chronic, blistering skin lesions in sun-exposed areas, often accompanied by increased skin fragility and hyperpigmentation. While genetic predisposition plays a role, environmental factors and comorbidities are crucial in its development.
b: Most common porphyria worldwide.
Characterized by photosensitive skin lesions, fragility, and hyperpigmentation.
Often triggered by environmental factors and co-existing conditions.

sections.p: Heme synthesis is a multi-step enzymatic pathway that produces heme, a crucial component of hemoglobin and cytochromes. In PCT, there is a deficiency in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), the fifth enzyme in this pathway. This enzyme converts uroporphyrinogen to coproporphyrinogen. When UROD activity is reduced, uroporphyrinogen and other porphyrin precursors accumulate.
b: Heme synthesis pathway produces heme, vital for oxygen transport and metabolism.
UROD enzyme deficiency is central to PCT pathogenesis.
Accumulation of uroporphyrinogen and related porphyrins occurs due to impaired conversion.

sections.p: UROD activity can be inhibited by various factors, leading to the manifestation of PCT. Iron overload is a significant contributor, as iron can oxidize uroporphyrinogen, making it a poor substrate for UROD. Other factors like alcohol, estrogens, and hepatitis C infection can also impair UROD function or increase porphyrin production, tipping the balance towards disease expression.
b: Iron overload is a key regulatory factor, inhibiting UROD activity.
Alcohol consumption can exacerbate porphyrin accumulation.
Estrogen use and hepatitis C infection are known triggers.

sections.p: The core problem in PCT is a functional deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. This can be inherited (Type II PCT, autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance) or acquired (Type I PCT, more common). The reduced enzyme activity leads to an accumulation of porphyrinogens, which are then oxidized to porphyrins. These porphyrins are photosensitive and, upon exposure to UV light, generate reactive oxygen species that damage skin cells, leading to the characteristic blistering and fragility.
b: Functional deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) is the root cause.
Type I (acquired) is more common than Type II (inherited) PCT.
Accumulated porphyrins become photoactivated by UV light, causing skin damage.

sections.p: Diagnosing PCT involves recognizing the characteristic skin lesions and confirming elevated porphyrin levels. Management focuses on reducing porphyrin levels and addressing underlying triggers. Phlebotomy is a cornerstone of treatment, as it reduces iron stores, thereby improving UROD activity. Avoiding alcohol and sun exposure, and treating associated conditions like hepatitis C, are also crucial.
b: Characteristic skin lesions are key to initial clinical suspicion.
Phlebotomy is a primary treatment to reduce iron overload.
Avoiding triggers like alcohol and sun exposure is vital for disease control.

t.b: Does the patient have elevated porphyrins? Elevated total plasma porphyrins, especially uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin, are indicative of PCT. If unavailable, urine porphyrin analysis can be used.
Which specific porphyrins are elevated? Markedly elevated uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin are characteristic of PCT. This helps differentiate from other porphyrias.
Are there specific porphyrin patterns in stool? Elevated isocoproporphyrin is highly suggestive of PCT. This can aid diagnosis, especially if urine tests are equivocal.

Is there evidence of iron overload? Elevated ferritin levels support the diagnosis and guide phlebotomy treatment. In low-resource settings, a therapeutic trial of phlebotomy can be considered if ferritin is high and other tests are unavailable.
Is there underlying liver damage or disease? Abnormal LFTs may indicate co-existing liver disease (e.g., hepatitis C, hemochromatosis), which can exacerbate PCT.
Is HCV infection a contributing factor? A positive result indicates a treatable trigger for PCT, common in many regions.
Is HIV infection a contributing factor? HIV can be associated with PCT, especially in high-prevalence areas, and its management is important for overall health.

sections.p: Remember that PCT is the most common porphyria and is often acquired, triggered by factors like iron overload, alcohol, and hepatitis C. The key enzyme deficiency is uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Phlebotomy is a primary treatment. Think about the clinical context and associated comorbidities, especially in diverse patient populations.
b: PCT is the most common porphyria, often acquired.
Key enzyme: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD).
Iron overload, alcohol, and hepatitis C are major triggers.
Phlebotomy is a first-line treatment.
Skin lesions are photosensitive subepidermal vesicles with vessel wall thickening.

faq.q: What is the main difference between Type I and Type II PCT?
faq.a: Type I PCT is acquired and more common, while Type II PCT is inherited due to a genetic mutation in the UROD gene, though it still often requires triggers to manifest.

faq.q: Why is phlebotomy an effective treatment for PCT?
faq.a: Phlebotomy reduces iron stores in the body. Excess iron inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, so reducing iron improves the enzyme's function and decreases porphyrin production.

While the underlying genetic predisposition for Type II PCT cannot be cured, the symptoms of PCT can be effectively managed and often brought into remission by treating triggers and reducing porphyrin levels.
